text:
NORA. Only to sew on my costume. Good heavens, how unreasonable you are.
(sits down on the sofa.) Now be good, Doctor Rank; tomorrow you shall
see how beautifully I shall dance; and then you must imagine that I am
doing it only for your sake—yes, and then, of course, for
Torvald’s—that goes without saying. (takes various things out of the box.)
Doctor Rank, sit down here, and I shall show you something.

RANK (sits down). What is it?

NORA. Look here. Look!

RANK. Silk stockings.

NORA. Flesh-colored. Aren’t they lovely? Yes, it is so dark
in here now; but tomorrow—. No, no, no; you may only see the foot. Oh
well, you may indeed see the upper part too, if you like.

RANK. Hm—

NORA. Why do you look so critical? Perhaps you don’t think
they will fit?

RANK. I cannot possibly have any well-founded opinion about
that.

NORA (looks at him for a moment). Shame on you. (taps him lightly
on the ear with the stockings.) That is what you get. (packs them up again.)

RANK. And what other delights am I to be allowed to see?

NORA. You will not be allowed to see another bit; for you
are naughty.

(she hums a little and searches among the things.)

RANK (after a brief silence). When I sit here like this,
quite intimately together with you, I cannot understand—no, I cannot
comprehend—what would have become of me if I had never come into this
house.

NORA (smiles). Oh, I think you are actually quite comfortable
with us.

RANK (more softly, staring ahead). And then to have to leave
all of it—

NORA. Nonsense; you are not leaving it.

RANK (as before). —and not even be able to leave behind one
poor token of gratitude; scarcely even a fleeting sense of loss—nothing
but an empty place that can be filled by the first person who comes along.

NORA. And if I were now to ask you to—? No—

RANK. To what?

NORA. For a great proof of your friendship—

RANK. Yes, yes?

NORA. No, I mean—for an immensely great service—

RANK. Would you really, for once, make me so happy?

NORA. Oh, you do not know at all what it is.

RANK. Very well, then; say it.

NORA. No, but I cannot, Doctor Rank; it is something so
unreasonably great—advice and help and a service, all at once—

RANK. So much the better. I cannot imagine what you can
mean. But do speak. Do I not have your confidence?

NORA. Yes, you do, as no one else does. You are my most
faithful and best friend; you know that well enough. That is why I will
tell you. Very well, then, Doctor Rank; there is something you must help
me prevent. You know how deeply, how indescribably dearly Torvald loves
me; never for a moment would he hesitate to give his life for my sake.

RANK (leaning toward her). Nora—do you think, then, that he
is the only one—?

NORA (with a slight start). Who—?

RANK. Who would gladly give his life for your sake.

NORA (heavily). I see.

RANK. I swore to myself that you should know it before I
went away. I would never find a better opportunity. Yes, Nora, now you
know it. And now you also know that you can confide in me as in no one
else.

NORA (rises; evenly and calmly). Let me pass.

RANK (makes room for her but remains seated). Nora—

NORA (in the doorway to the hall). Helen, bring in the lamp.
—(goes over toward the stove.) Oh, dear Doctor Rank, that was really
horrid of you.

RANK (rises). That I have loved you every bit as deeply as
anyone else has? Was that horrid?

NORA. No, but that you should go and tell me. There was no
need at all—

RANK. What do you mean? Did you know, then—?

(The maid enters with the lamp, puts it on the table, and goes out again.)

RANK. Nora—Mrs. Helmer—I ask you, did you know anything?

NORA. Oh, how do I know what I knew or did not know? I
really cannot tell you—. How could you be so clumsy, Doctor Rank!
Everything was so good as it was.

RANK. Well, at any rate, you now know for certain that I am
at your disposal, body and soul. And will you speak freely now?

NORA (looks at him). After this?

RANK. I beg you, let me know what it is.

NORA. You cannot be told anything now.

RANK. Yes, yes. You must not punish me like this. Let me be
allowed to do for you whatever lies within human power.

NORA. Now you can do nothing for me. Besides, I am sure I
do not need any help. You will see that it is all merely imagination.
Yes, surely that is so. Of course! (sits down in the rocking chair,
looks at him, smiles.) Well, you certainly are a fine gentleman, Doctor
Rank. Don’t you think you ought to be ashamed of yourself now that the
lamp has come in?

RANK. No; not really. But perhaps I should go—for good?

NORA. No, you certainly must not do that. Naturally, you
must come here as before. You know very well that Torvald cannot do
without you.

RANK. Yes, but you?

NORA. Oh, I always think it becomes tremendously pleasant
here when you come.

RANK. That is precisely what led me astray. You are a riddle
to me. Many a time it has seemed to me that you would almost as soon be
with me as with Helmer.

NORA. Yes, you see, there are some people whom one loves
most, and other people whom one would almost rather be with.

RANK. Ah yes, there is something in that.

NORA. When I was at home, I naturally loved Papa most. But
I always thought it was so immensely amusing when I could steal down to
the maids’ room; for they did not lecture me in the least, and they
always talked so amusingly among themselves.

RANK. Aha; so it is they whom I have replaced.

NORA (springs up and goes over to him). Oh, dear, kind Doctor
Rank, that is not at all what I meant. But surely you can understand
that with Torvald it is just as it was with Papa—

(The maid enters from the hall.)

MAID. Madam! (whispers and hands her a card.)

NORA (glances at the card). Ah! (puts it in her pocket.)

RANK. Is something wrong?

NORA. No, no, not at all; it is only something—it is my new
costume—

RANK. What do you mean? Your costume is lying right there.

NORA. Oh yes, that one; but there is another; I have ordered
it—Torvald must not know about it—

RANK. Aha, so there we have the great secret.

NORA. Yes, indeed; just go in to him; he is sitting in the
inner room; keep him occupied for a while—

RANK. Do not worry; he shall not get away from me. (he goes
into Helmer’s room.)

NORA (to the maid). And he is standing waiting in the kitchen?

MAID. Yes, he came up the back stairs—

NORA. But did you not tell him that someone was here?

MAID. Yes, but it did no good.

NORA. He will not go away again?

MAID. No, he will not go until he has spoken with Madam.
